summary: White tower on Seal Island off southwest Nova Scotia, first lit 28 Nov 1831; the Hichens and Crowell keepers, the 1843 Columbia wreck and 1990 unwatching.

lens.where: Seal Island Light Museum, Barrington, N.S. (replica top of the tower)

structures.note: Begun 1830 on a stone and mortar foundation; first lit 28 Nov 1831. Lighthouse Friends gives sixty feet from base to vane; NSLPS gives 67 feet. Lantern replaced 1862 and again 1978.
Built on the extreme south point, 585 ft from the light, to replace the building beside the light.
For the keeper and his assistant.

staffing.note: Keepers' families moved off the island by 1986 (rotational teams). Unwatched from 17 Oct 1990.

access.note: Reached only by boat. Grounds open, tower closed.

events.note: Construction began (NSLPS). New Brunswick agreed in 1830 to pay toward the cost (LF).
First lit on the night of 28 Nov 1831 (NSLPS). Completed 1831 at the cost of 1,009 pounds (LF).
A bell placed at the station for fog (LF).
New lantern room installed atop the tower (LF).
Power steam whistle placed in operation in August 1870 (LF).
Second-order Fresnel lens from France placed in operation from 25 Oct 1870 (LF).
Reservoir built; its brick walls fell in within months (LF).
Government life-saving station established: 'Seal Island station. Established 1880' (Department of Marine report).
Corning Crowell replaced his father Thomas as keeper (LF).
Fog whistle moved to a new building 585 ft south of the light; in operation 16 Feb 1903 (LF; 1903 report).

New second-order lens (LF: three flashes every fifteen seconds). The 1907 report calls the new light a 'second order double flashing light' being installed; the 1908 report calls it triple. See resolved_conflicts.
Two red horizontal bands painted on the white tower (LF).
Subsidized volunteer crew called out to the wreck of the schooner Maia (Department report 1913-14).
Oil plant replaced the steam fog-alarm plant (LF).
Double dwelling built for the keeper and assistant (LF).
Iron lantern room and Fresnel lens removed; DCB 36 rotating beacon and aluminum lantern installed. Old lantern and lens taken to Barrington (LF; NSLPS).

keepers.name: H. Hitchins
keepers.note: Coxswain of the Seal Island life-saving station (Department of Marine). Printed as 'H. Hitchins' in the 1905 report (cite 11, printed p. 141). The 1903 report's OCR reads 'H. Kitchens, coxswain' (cite 10). The 1901 station table reads 'H. Hitchens' only by column position (cite 9, scan 173, printed 62), not checked against the page image, so the line starts in 1903.

wrecks.outcome: Struck the rock later named Blonde Rock. Crew and prisoners reached Seal Island in boats; the privateers Scammell and Lively arrived days later (LF).

Struck Black Ledge in fog near Seal Island. The day is disputed: the Boston Transcript (reprinted in the Republican Herald, 12 July 1843) says Monday afternoon; the mail officer's letter dated Seal Island, 4 July, says Sunday at a quarter past one. The letter says the master of Seal Island Light came alongside and that passengers were landed on the island; the Transcript says fishing vessels took passengers, mails and baggage to the mainland. The Missouri Radical records a subscription and thanks to the islanders and the keeper (spelled Hitchings).
Went ashore on Blonde Rock in late April 1869, bound Portland to Glasgow with wheat. Crew taken off and landed at Barrington; hull and cargo sold at auction (LF).
Wreck attended by the Seal Island volunteer crew (Department report 1913-14).

wrecks.vessel: Collision off Seal Island (S.S. Borghild and S.S. Oriole)
wrecks.outcome: Four of the Oriole's crew lost. Formal investigation at Halifax on 18-19 August (1916 report): the master and mate of the Borghild found in default for Rules of the Road Art. 16; the master of the Oriole also found in default.
Stranded on the Limb Ledge off Seal Island and became a total wreck (Department report 1923-24).

corrections.current: 2026 built (Year of the tower described by the Lighthouse Directory)
corrections.why: No source dates a build to 2026. Construction began 1830 and the light was first lit 28 Nov 1831 (NSLPS; LF). The 2026 entry looks like a data error.

corrections.current: 1831 built (Year of the tower described by the Lighthouse Directory)
corrections.why: The first-lit night is the best-sourced date; the 1831 build date is the completion year (LF).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1830 and 1831. NSLPS says construction began in 1830 and the light was first lit on 28 Nov 1831. LF says the light was completed in 1831. These are the start and end of the same tower, not two towers.

The sources give different characteristics because the light has changed over time: a group of three flashes every 15 s from 1907 (LF), 'Flashing White' in 1992 (NSLPS), and Fl W 10s in the current Coast Guard list (cite 4).

The Boston Transcript, reprinted in the Providence Republican Herald of 12 July 1843, says the Columbia struck Black Ledge on Monday afternoon. The mail officer's letter printed in the same paper, dated Seal Island 4 July, says she grounded on Sunday at a quarter past one. The story gives both; the record's date is set to July 1843 without a day.

The 1907 report says a second order double flashing light is being installed at Seal Island; the 1908 report says the new second order triple flashing light was put in operation. Lighthouse Friends gives three flashes every fifteen seconds from 1907. The story gives both reports and states the disagreement.
The 1923-24 report names the ledge as 'Limb ledge (Seal island, N.S.)' in its movements section (p. 85) and as 'Black ledge' in a radio note (p. 151). The story gives both.

The NSLPS page gives this light as 'Operating: This light is operational' in its panel and 'Still Operating: No' in its summary table. The Coast Guard list gives the light as Fl W 10s. The story reports the NSLPS inconsistency rather than choosing one.

notes_for_editor: Fact-checked 2026-10-27. Changed: Columbia's day is now stated as disputed (Transcript Monday afternoon; the mail officer's letter Sunday at a quarter past one); the 1907 double vs 1908 triple flashing light is stated; the Aberdeen's ledge is Limb ledge in the movements section (p. 85) and Black ledge in a radio note (p. 151); the NSLPS page contradicts itself on operating status ('This light is operational' vs 'Still Operating: No'), and the story says so; the 1978 lantern removal has no named agent in any source, so the story no longer names the Coast Guard. Keeper dates still disagree between Lighthouse Friends and the NSLPS list (Hichens, Edmund Crowell, Corning Crowell, John Crowell, Hamilton); both are cited and the story says so. Height disagrees (60 ft LF, 67 ft NSLPS). H. Hitchins (coxswain): printed 'H. Hitchins' in the 1905 report (cite 11); the 1903 report's OCR reads 'H. Kitchens' (cite 10); the 1901 table reads 'H. Hitchens' by column position (cite 9, scan 173, printed 62) and was not checked against the page image, so the line starts in 1903. The 1916 collision's second vessel is the Oriole (vessel list and finding, OCR). The 1913-14 Maia entry is at scan p. 220; the printed page is not confirmed (corpus page returns '21?'). The 1843 keeper is printed as Hitchins (letter) and Hitchings (Radical); no source links him to Richard Hichens by name, so the story does not. Not used: Wikipedia; NSLPS 'Began 1827' and '1922-1941 second-order lens' lines (conflict with LF and the reports); 'Seal Island Pole Light' and 'Seal Island, Lennox Passage' entries (different stations). The 1991 heritage-designation date was not checked (Federal Heritage Building page id=3930 did not render). Post-1960 keepers appear only in the roster, as Lighthouse Friends prints them.
